title: Make It Move
tagline: Your first physical computer reacts to you.
objectives: I can explain the difference between an input and an output using real examples.
I can build a working program on a real micro:bit that reacts to an input.
I can test my program and use what happens (or doesn't) to find and fix problems myself.

config.headline: Today you make a computer react.
lines: In this lesson you will learn what an INPUT and an OUTPUT are — and you will prove you know, by building a tiny computer that reacts when you press it.

Look at the three photos below. A lift button, a pedestrian crossing, a fitness tracker: something happens (the INPUT — a press, a step), and something reacts (the OUTPUT — the doors open, the green man lights, the step count goes up). Every machine you have ever used works on that one idea.

The computer in your hands today is called a micro:bit — a computer the size of a biscuit, with two buttons and a grid of 25 tiny lights. You will work in a pair with the person sitting beside you, one micro:bit between the two of you, and together you will TELL it how to react: press a button, get a picture; shake it, get a ghost.

By the end of the hour you will have built a program on a real device, tested it with your own hands, and learned the first rule of every programmer's life: when it doesn't work, the code is trying to tell you something.

config.title: The Signal Relay Ladder
config.intro: This is where you learn to BUILD — and you do it in your pair: you and the person beside you, one micro:bit between you. The ladder has four small challenges, called rungs, and you climb them in order. Each rung card tells you exactly what your program should do. You build it in MakeCode (in your other tab), copy it onto the micro:bit, and test it with your own hands. Nobody marks this — the device itself is the judge: either it does what the card says, or it doesn't, and you can both see which. Take turns: one of you builds the blocks, the other holds the card and runs the test. Swap jobs at every rung.

unplugged.title: Rung 1 — The Human Circuit
lines: This first rung needs no computer at all: you and your partner are going to BE the machine. Stand up.

Every machine from the start of the lesson — the lift, the crossing, the step-counter — has a part that NOTICES something happen (computing calls it a SENSOR) and a part that REACTS (an ACTUATOR). Decide now: one of you is the sensor, the other is the actuator.
SENSOR: mime pressing an invisible button. ACTUATOR: the instant you see the press, throw both arms up — you are the heart appearing on the screen.
New signal! SENSOR: mime shaking a device. ACTUATOR: wave both hands — you are the message scrolling across the screen.
Swap jobs and run both signals again, so each of you has played both parts.
Finish by saying it out loud together: the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT. Those three words run the whole hour.
unplugged.confirm: We both played Sensor and Actuator — and said the magic sentence
soloLines: This first rung needs no computer at all — and no partner on a catch-up: YOU are the whole machine, both parts of it.
Every machine from the start of the lesson has a part that NOTICES something happen (a SENSOR) and a part that REACTS (an ACTUATOR). Today you play both.
With one hand, mime pressing an invisible button. The instant you do, throw your other arm up — that's the heart appearing on the screen.
New signal: mime shaking a device with one hand, and wave the other — that's the message scrolling across.

Finish by saying it out loud (quietly counts): the press is the INPUT. The reaction is the OUTPUT. The rule connecting them — when THIS happens, do THAT — is an EVENT. Those three words run the whole hour.
unplugged.soloConfirm: I ran both signals — and said the magic sentence

rungs.title: Rung 2 — First Signal
rungs.target: Your challenge: make the micro:bit show a HEART icon whenever button A is pressed.
rungs.test: Copy your program onto the micro:bit: press Download in MakeCode, then drag the downloaded file onto the MICROBIT drive — the film button below replays exactly how, if you need it. Then press the real button A. Did the heart appear? (If your device won't connect, the on-screen simulator counts while your teacher sorts it.)
rungs.hint: Is your 'show icon' block sitting INSIDE the 'on button A pressed' block? A block floating on its own never runs.

rungs.title: Rung 3 — Two Signals
rungs.target: Your challenge: give the micro:bit TWO different reactions — press button A and a HEART appears; press button B and a HAPPY FACE appears.
rungs.test: Copy it across, then press A, then B. Do you get two DIFFERENT pictures — heart for A, happy face for B?
rungs.hint: You need TWO separate 'on button pressed' blocks — one set to A, one set to B. Check the little dropdown on each one.

rungs.title: Rung 4 — The Vanishing Ghost
rungs.target: Your challenge: when the micro:bit is SHAKEN, this is what should happen: 1. a GHOST icon appears — 2. it stays on screen for one second — 3. the screen clears itself.
rungs.test: Copy it across and give it a real shake. Does the ghost appear, hold, then vanish cleanly — every single time? Now prove the pause is earning its place: take the pause block out, copy the program across again, and shake. The ghost seems never to appear at all — the clear wipes it before your eyes can catch it. Put the pause back.
rungs.hint: The ORDER inside 'on shake' matters: show icon, THEN pause (ms) 1000, THEN clear screen. The pause is the only thing giving the ghost time on screen — without it, 'clear screen' wipes it before your eyes can catch it and you see nothing at all. (Rung 2's heart stayed put because nothing came along to clear it.)

stretch.title: Stretch — Two Buttons at Once
stretch.target: Your stretch challenge: see if you can make one input trigger a whole SEQUENCE. When A and B are pressed at the SAME TIME, this is what should happen: 1. a heart appears — 2. it holds for half a second — 3. a happy face takes its place.
stretch.test: Copy it across and press A + B together on the real device. Heart, half-second pause, then happy face — every single time?

config.introSolo: This is where you learn to BUILD — on your own today, so you play both parts yourself. The ladder has four small challenges, called rungs, and you climb them in order. Each rung card tells you exactly what your program should do: build it in MakeCode (in your other tab, or the on-screen simulator), then run the real test yourself. Nobody marks this — the device is still the judge.
config.help: Read the rung card, build what it asks for in MakeCode (its own tab), then TEST it for real — press the button, do the shake. If it worked, press the gold button and the next rung appears. Stuck? That's what the Debug Hint is for — it costs 2 XP and nudges you toward the fix without giving it away. The film button replays the MakeCode film without losing your place.

config.title: Bank your build
config.intro: A build that lives on one computer is a build you can lose. In this step you learn the habit that protects every piece of work you ever make in DT: save it to your Google Drive — the Vault from Lesson 1 — and it follows your login to ANY machine, even at home. The website will then genuinely check your Drive and only give the badge when the file is really there.

steps.title: Download your build
steps.text: In MakeCode press the purple Download button. A file ending in .hex lands in the computer's Downloads folder — that file IS your program.

steps.title: Open your Vault
steps.text: New tab → drive.google.com → open School → DT Work. Don't see those folders? Tap + New → Folder, make 'School', open it, make 'DT Work' inside — thirty seconds, then carry on.

steps.title: Drag it in
steps.text: Drag the .hex file from Downloads into DT Work. Done — the website can now verify it's really there.

config.passText: Your build now follows your login anywhere — that's the whole point of the Vault. Next lesson you can pick up exactly where you left off, on any machine.
config.failText: Not there yet. Check each step above — especially that the file went INTO the DT Work folder, not just onto the desktop — then run the inspection again.
config.help: Three steps: download your program from MakeCode, open your Google Drive in a new tab, drag the file into School → DT Work. Then press the inspection button and the website checks your Drive for real. If it says the file isn't there, check it went INSIDE the DT Work folder, not just onto the desktop.

config.intro: Two scenarios before you go — and unlike everything else today, these ARE marked: your teacher sees how the class did, so think like a debugger before you tap.

items.stem: You build 'on button A pressed → show heart'. You press button A on the micro:bit but nothing appears. What is the MOST likely reason?
options: You forgot to flash the code onto the device
Button A only works if you press button B at the same time

items.stem: Your finished program: press button A → a heart appears on the LED grid. Which part is the INPUT?

config.help: Two marked questions about today. Answer on your own — your teacher sees how the class did. Your verdicts arrive once the whole report is filed, at the end of the last screen.

config.intro: Last one: four real blocks, one working program. Put them in the order that matches the sentence — you spent today learning why order inside an event matters.

item.prompt: When you shake it, a ghost appears on the screen, holds for one second, then the screen clears.

config.help: Tap blocks from the tray into your program, in the order the sentence describes. Check when you're sure — you'll be shown the working order if it's off.
